questions.q: Define "disengagement theory" of ageing and state its core proposition about the older person–society relationship.
questions.a: Disengagement theory (Cumming & Henry, 1961) proposes that mutual withdrawal between older adults and society is inevitable, universal, and functional — society benefits from orderly transfer of roles, and the elder benefits from reduced responsibilities. A wrong answer (e.g., "disengagement is pathological and must be prevented") reveals the student confuses the theory's descriptive claim with the activity theory's normative prescription, and misses that disengagement theory was historically influential in shaping early retirement policies.

questions.q: A 68-year-old retired engineer joins a senior citizens' trekking group, learns smartphone photography, and volunteers at a community library. Using activity theory and continuity theory, explain why this pattern supports successful ageing — and identify one limitation of activity theory in the Indian urban context.
questions.a: Activity theory: maintained roles/activities preserve self-concept and life satisfaction (he replaces work role with volunteer/trekker roles). Continuity theory: he sustains internal structures (competence, curiosity) and external structures (social participation) from midlife. Limitation: activity theory assumes access to resources (health, transport, safe parks, digital literacy) — many Indian urban elderly lack these due to poverty, poor infrastructure, or caregiving duties, making "activity" a privilege not a universal option. A wrong answer that only lists activities without linking to theoretical mechanisms shows surface-level understanding.

questions.q: Mrs. Rao, 75, lives alone after her husband's death. Her daughter insists she move to a "premium senior living community" with medical facilities and scheduled activities. Mrs. Rao refuses, saying "I want to die in my own home." Apply socioemotional selectivity theory (SST) and the concept of "ageing in place" to analyse her resistance, and propose a compromise that respects her autonomy while addressing safety.
questions.a: SST: with limited time perspective, she prioritises emotionally meaningful goals (familiar home, memories, autonomy) over knowledge-acquisition goals (new friends, facilities). "Ageing in place" reflects identity continuity and environmental mastery. Compromise: home modifications (grab bars, emergency alert), weekly nurse visits, and a "buddy system" with neighbours — preserving her preferred environment while mitigating risk. A wrong answer focusing only on "stubbornness" or "safety first" ignores the motivational shift SST describes and violates the MWPSC Act's emphasis on elderly's right to choose residence.

questions.q: Compare the psychosocial outcomes of "institutionalisation" vs "family care" for Indian elderly using Erikson's integrity vs despair and the concept of "filial piety". Why might a well-run old age home produce better integrity outcomes than a neglectful family setting?
questions.a: Integrity requires life review yielding acceptance and wisdom; despair arises from regret and bitterness. In a neglectful family (elder ignored, finances controlled, caregiving perfunctory), the elder experiences role loss + relational betrayal → despair. A quality institution offering peer community, structured reminiscence therapy, and resident autonomy in daily choices can foster integrity through new generative roles (mentoring, storytelling) and dignity. Filial piety as obligation without affect breeds resentment; care quality matters more than care setting. A wrong answer idealising "family care" as universally superior ignores NCERT data on elder abuse and the feminisation of caregiving burden.

questions.q: Critique the National Policy for Older Persons (1999) and the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act (2007) from a psychosocial perspective. Identify one gap where the policy assumes a family structure that no longer exists for many urban elderly.
questions.a: NPOP 1999 assumes multigenerational co-residence and family as primary caregiver — but 30% elderly are below poverty line, 80% rural, and feminisation means widowed women often lack property rights. MWPSC Act 2007 mandates children/relatives to maintain parents, but enforcement is weak, and "maintenance" is narrowly financial (food, shelter, medical) — ignoring psychosocial needs (companionship, respect, autonomy). Gap: both policies assume adult children are available/willing caregivers; they don't address childless elderly, migrant children, or daughters-in-law as primary caregivers (gendered burden). A wrong answer listing only financial provisions misses the psychosocial dimension central to Home Science.

questions.q: Design a community-based "Active Ageing" programme for a mixed-income urban neighbourhood that integrates: (a) socioemotional selectivity principles, (b) intergenerational contact, and (c) low-cost resource mobilisation. Specify three activities, their theoretical rationale, and one measurable outcome per activity.
questions.a:
1. **"Life Story Circles"** (weekly, 90 min): elders share themed memories (festivals, work, migration) with college volunteers recording digital archives. Rationale: SST — emotionally meaningful reminiscence; generativity (Erikson). Outcome: 80% participants report "sense of legacy" on post-session Likert scale.
2. **"Skill-Swap Workshops"** (monthly): elders teach traditional cooking/crafts; youth teach smartphone/UPI/banking. Rationale: continuity theory (internal/external structure maintenance); reciprocity reduces power imbalance. Outcome: 50% elders independently complete one digital transaction post-workshop.
3. **"Neighbourhood Walk & Talk"** (biweekly): guided walks in local park with health screening kiosk. Rationale: activity theory + ageing in place (environmental mastery); low-cost (public space, ASHA workers). Outcome: 30% increase in self-reported outdoor mobility at 3 months.
A poor answer lists generic "yoga, bhajan, medical camp" without theoretical anchoring or measurable outcomes.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Late adulthood (typically 60+ years in India) is the final stage of the lifespan characterised by progressive physiological decline, shifting social roles (retirement, ______, widowhood), and the psychosocial task of achieving ego integrity versus despair (Erikson), requiring adaptive strategies to maintain well-being despite losses in health, status, and social networks.
Fill in the blank: Imagine your 72-year-old ______ recently lost her husband, retired from teaching, and now lives alone in a metro city while her children work abroad.

Fill in the blank: Late adulthood (typically ______+ years in India) is the final stage of the lifespan characterised by progressive physiological decline, shifting social roles (retirement, grandparenting, widowhood), and the psychosocial task of achieving ego integrity versus despair (Erikson), requiring adaptive strategies to maintain well-being despite losses in health, status, and social networks.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can compare and contrast at least three major ageing theories (disengagement, activity, continuity, socioemotional selectivity), apply Erikson's integrity vs despair to case scenarios, and design a multi-component psychosocial intervention for an elderly person facing retirement, bereavement, and health decline.
